children.html: Body image flexibility contributes to explaining the link between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation in White college-bound females
University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Department of Psychology, Health Psychology Ph.D. Program, 9201, University City Blvd., Charlotte, NC 28223, USA
Article history: Received 12 October 2014 Received in revised form 17 May 2015 Accepted 1 June 2015
Keywords: Body dissatisfaction Body appreciation Body image flexibility BMI White older adolescent females

Limited research has provided a theoretically-driven accounting of the association between negative and positive body image occurring within persons nor clarified what factors may contribute to explaining this relationship. To address this gap in the existing literature, the present study, guided by an overarching affect regulation theoretical framework, evaluated the potential indirect effect of body dissatisfaction on body appreciation via body image flexibility in a college-bound sample of 84 White older adolescent females. Participants provided self-reported height and weight, which were used to calculate body mass index (BMI) and completed the Body Image-Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (BI-AAQ; Sandoz, Wilson, Merwin, & Kellum, 2013) as a measure of body image flexibility and the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005). Body dissatisfaction was operationalized as three types of body size discrepancy scores (i.e., current minus personal ideal, current minus cultural ideal, current minus typical female ethnic peer) using Pulvers' Figure Rating Scale (Pulvers et al., 2004). In all models tested, body image flexibility partially mediated the associations between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation. Results were retained controlling for BMI. Preliminary findings suggest that at this developmental juncture, bolstering body image flexibility affect regulation skills may be an optimal target for supporting body appreciation when body dissatisfaction is elicited by internal and external body image threats.

Affect regulation constitutes a widely accepted theoretical accounting of the functional association between negatively-valenced internal experiences and eating disturbances (e.g., Anestis, Selby, Fink, & Joiner, 2007; Heatherton & Baumeister, 1991; Polivy & Herman, 1993; Stice, Shaw, & Nemeroff, 1998). Indeed, considerable evidence has substantiated framing disordered eating as maladaptive behavioral strategies arising as attempts to control (e.g., suppress, avoid, escape) the aversive experience of stress, negative emotions and critical self-evaluations including those stemming from body dissatisfaction (e.g., Corstorphine, Mountford, Tomlinson, Waller, & Meyer, 2007; Heatherton & Baumeister, 1991; Whiteside et al., 2007). Such coping responses are sustained due to their ability to alleviate distress in the short-term at the expense of long-term impairments to health and well-being (Corstorphine et al., 2007). Recently, researchers have advanced this conceptualization towards enhancing our understanding of the relationship between aspects of negative and positive body

image (Cash, Santos, & Williams, 2005; Webb, Butler-Ajibade, & Robinson, 2014). Authors viewed this contribution as timely in the extant literature as current scholarship seeks to better clarify how dimensions of negative and positive body image unfold within persons (e.g., Atkinson & Wade, 2012; Svaldi, Naumann, Trentowska, Lackner, & Tuschen-Caffier, 2013) and by extension how positive body image may attenuate risk for eating pathology as predicted by body dissatisfaction (e.g., Ferreira, Pinto-Gouveia, & Duarte, 2011).

These contemporary affect regulation models propose to offer a theoretically-driven approach to explaining how and why negative and positive body image operate synergistically within individuals (as an alternative to viewing these dimensions of body image as simply de-contextualized polar opposites; Tylka, 2011). Adopting this modern perspective holds promise in identifying targets for promoting more adaptive ways of relating to one's body which in turn could yield additional benefits in the realms of eating (e.g., Avalos & Tylka, 2006; Sandoz, Wilson, Merwin, & Kellum, 2013; Schoenefeld & Webb, 2013; Wendell, Masuda, & Le, 2012), exercise (e.g., Homan & Tylka, 2014), and other health-protective behaviors (Andrew, Tiggemann, & Clark, 2014; Gillen, 2015). Aligned with this nascent perspective, the current preliminary investigation aimed to evaluate an extension of Webb et al.'s (2014) affect

regulation model of positive body image. Specifically, this analysis sought to ascertain whether a newly-introduced form of positive body image (i.e., body image flexibility; Sandoz et al., 2013) mediated the associations between body size discrepancy metrics of body dissatisfaction and another more well-established facet of positive body image (i.e., body appreciation; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a) in a sample of White older adolescent females on the developmental cusp of preparing to transition to early college life.

Webb et al.'s (2014) affect regulation model of positive body image proposed combining conceptual features from Cash et al.'s (2005) coping with body image threats framework and from psychological flexibility theory derived from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT; Hayes, Strosahl, & Wilson, 1999). The core components of each are briefly outlined here. Drawing upon Lazarus and Folkman's (1984) earlier appraisal-based stress and coping model, Cash et al. (2005) described three potential affect regulation strategies to capture how individuals may typically respond in the face of everyday affronts to body image. These coping styles include: (a) avoidance (e.g., cognitive or overt behaviors designed to distract, remove oneself from or otherwise disconnect from the ongoing experience of body image-related distress), (b) appearance fixing (e.g., attempts to hide, camouflage or conceal aspects of one's physical appearance to mitigate distress), and (c) positive rational acceptance (e.g., internal self-talk intended to remind the individual of their other non-appearance-based positive attributes or to reassure oneself that the distressing experience is temporary and will subside; Cash et al., 2005). Research has shown that higher levels of avoidant and appearance fixing coping correspond with higher levels of self-objectification, body shame, depressive symptoms, and disordered eating attitudes in conjunction with lower subjective well-being in college women (Choma, Shove, Busseri, Sadava, & Hosker, 2009). Conversely, positive rational acceptance coping tended to demonstrate an opposite pattern of effects (Choma et al., 2009) and was also shown to attenuate the link between body image concerns and depressive symptoms in a large adolescent community sample (Hughes & Gullone, 2011).

While psychological flexibility serves as the cornerstone of ACT's functional contextualism philosophy (i.e., to understand the behavior one must be able to deconstruct its associations with situational reinforcers) for promoting human flourishing (Ciarrochi, Kashdan, & Harris, 2013). It is characterized by an open, receptive mindset that is intentionally deployed to support the individual's capacity to actively persist towards living a meaningful, values-congruent life when encountering the normative human experiences of pain and suffering (Hayes et al., 1999). Possessing similar qualities to the aforementioned positive rational acceptance coping response style (Cash et al., 2005), this mindful and compassionate stance contrasts experiential avoidance (akin to Cash et al.'s 2005 avoidant coping strategy) or the general tendency to want to avert, modify, or otherwise create distance from thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, and emotions one perceives as intolerable or unacceptable to experience (Callaghan, Sandoz, Darrow, & Feeney, 2015; Hayes et al., 1999).

Therefore, rigidly engaging in experiential avoidance runs counter to being able to act consistently with one's most deeply held values while cultivating greater psychological flexibility serves as the antidote (Hayes et al., 1999). Additionally, research indicates that high experiential avoidance (or psychological inflexibility) corresponds with higher levels of negative emotionality, reported psychopathology along with poorer quality of life in both patient and non-clinical adult samples (Gamez et al., 2014). In fact, evidence now suggests that it would be advantageous to consider viewing experiential avoidance/psychological inflexibility as a potent transdiagnostic factor influencing the development
and course of a broad range of clinical disorders (e.g., Spinhoven, Drost, de Rooij, van Hemert, & Penninx, 2014).

Drawing together these theoretical foundations within an integrative framework in the particular experiential domain of body image, Webb and colleagues' (2014) adapted model explained that individuals encounter myriad daily opportunities to confront threats to how they experience their bodies (Cash et al., 2005). Consequently, these internally- or externally-generated body image stressors activate self-evaluative social/body comparison processes (Festinger, 1954) relevant to noting self-discrepancies (Higgins, 1987) between their current body size and those of an internalized personal ideal standard, a typical ethnic peer referent, and/or for example a cultural (e.g., media) ideal (Webb et al., 2014). These perceptions may then simultaneously trigger body dissatisfaction in the form of harsh self-critical thoughts and negative emotions (e.g., shame, sadness, anxiety). As an alternative to engaging in experiential avoidance coping (Cash et al., 2005; Hayes et al., 1999), these authors suggested that more adaptive responses to body dissatisfaction as it is unfolding involved willingly embracing this aversive body image content with mindful and compassionate awareness (i.e., body image flexibility; Sandoz et al., 2013) and engaging in more frequent values-consistent behavior specifically with respect to adaptively relating to one's body (i.e., body appreciation; Avalos et al., 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a).

Body image flexibility shares conceptual foundations with ACT's (Hayes et al., 1999) more broad-based psychological flexibility construct as applied to the context of body image (Sandoz et al., 2013). Relatedly, it holds conceptual overlap with elements of a positive rational acceptance style in coping with body image-related stressors (Cash et al., 2005). Specifically, body image flexibility reflects openly engaging painful or unwanted thoughts and emotions regarding one's body size, shape or weight with mindful acceptance in the service of maintaining motivation to pursue and attain values-driven goals (e.g., going on an interview for a highly desirable job with the potential for increased income despite having serious concerns about one's weight; Sandoz et al., 2013). Experts have framed body image flexibility as a potential therapeutic change mechanism in the treatment of eating disturbances (Sandoz et al., 2013), which was corroborated in a naturalistic study of factors associated with reductions in eating pathology among women participating in an intensive residential eating disorder treatment program (Butryn et al., 2013). Moreover, a series of published findings supports the adaptive self-regulatory qualities of body image flexibility in the contexts of eating and embodiment (see Webb et al., 2014 for a brief summary and discussion). Recently, authors have proposed consideration of body image flexibility as a modern form of positive body image (Webb et al., 2014; Webb, Wood-Barcalow, & Tylka, 2015) that complements the experience of body appreciation (Avalos et al., 2005).

As its rapidly mounting scholarship base attests, body appreciation is widely recognized as the leading component of contemporary positive body image (Avalos et al., 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a, 2015b; Webb et al., 2015). It reflects an internalized mindset and behavioral orientation marked by proactively: (a) accepting one's body with all of its flaws and imperfections regardless of size, (b) respecting the body by attending to its needs, (c) protecting the body by resisting unrealistic and narrowly-defined standards of beauty and attractiveness promulgated in the media, and (d) by taking care of and nurturing the body's vitality through practicing health-promoting behaviors (Avalos et al., 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). A host of cross-cultural evidence supports body appreciation's positive links with multiple aspects of well-being (e.g., self-compassion, intuitive eating, optimism, life satisfaction, positive affect, and physical activity) and its inverse associations with disturbances in
psychological functioning (e.g., eating pathology, maladaptive perfectionism, and negative emotionality; see Tylka & Wood-Barcalow (2015a) for an overview).

In Webb et al.'s (2014) earlier study, both measures of positive body image were analyzed as criterion variables in separate models. Nevertheless, researchers at the time surmised that body image flexibility affect regulation skills may facilitate actualizing body appreciation values in the context of experiencing body dissatisfaction, yet this hypothesis remained untested (Webb et al., 2014). Capitalizing on this recommended future research direction, the current analysis desired to extend this original model by testing body image flexibility as a potential intermediary process variable that may help account for the inverse relationship between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation, which has been re-conceptualized here as valued action in line with psychological flexibility theory (Hayes et al., 1999). Thus, from an affect regulation process standpoint, body image flexibility may serve to enable individuals to more skillfully and compassionately accept the negative affect arising from perceived body size discrepancies, which in turn may promote greater commitment to continue to act in accordance with one's values by choosing to actively appreciate the body.

Emerging evidence from body image flexibility's cumulative empirical base supports the relevance of exploring this alternative indirect effect model in the untapped domain of explaining the association between negative and positive body image. First, body image flexibility was shown to partially mediate the links between disordered eating cognitions and self-reported eating pathology (Wendell et al., 2012) and between body dissatisfaction and disordered eating behavior (Sandoz et al., 2013) among college students. Timko and colleagues similarly observed significant indirect effects of negative body image on both symptoms of bulimia and drive for thinness via body image flexibility in both college and community adult female samples (Timko, Juarascio, Martin, Faherty, & Kalodner, 2014). Importantly, these effects were retained when global levels of psychological flexibility and a conceptually similar measure of body image avoidance were included in separate regression models (Timko et al., 2014). Finally, path analytic findings from another recent investigation indicated that this approach to relating to one's negative body image-related internal experiences fully mediated the association between the tendency to compare one's physical appearance to peers and the frequency of engaging in an inflexible eating style (Ferreira, Trindade, & Martinho, 2015).

Whereas, in the context of positive well-being, other evidence has demonstrated that body image flexibility helps explain the association between self-compassion and intuitive eating (Tylka, 2006) in undergraduate females (Schoenefeld & Webb, 2013). Additionally, in a large-scale survey of Dutch women, researchers reported a significant indirect effect of body comparison scores on reports of body satisfaction (i.e., a conventional, first-generation measure of positive body image) through mindfulness, which is considered a core feature of body image flexibility (Dijkstra & Barelds, 2011). Collectively, this amalgam of research supports body image flexibility's potential explanatory role in the domain of eating behavior. Nonetheless, the present investigation aims to provide a novel albeit preliminary analysis of how it might function in relation to facilitating another, more behaviorally-defined component of positive body image (i.e., body appreciation) in the context of coping with self-discrepancy-derived body dissatisfaction.

A pre-college sample of White older adolescent females was selected as the target demographic in which to investigate the primary study aim for the following reasons. First, although negative body image certainly does not discriminate based on race/ ethnicity or gender, research consistently reveals that younger

women who identify as White or Caucasian tend to report higher levels of body dissatisfaction relative to their ethnic minority female peers (e.g., Roberts, Cash, Feingold, & Johnson, 2006) and less body areas satisfaction than their male peers (e.g., Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2012). Secondly, the transition to college life is regarded as a potentially critical window in body image development among older adolescents (e.g., Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2012). This juncture is marked by attempts to effectively negotiate heightened appearance-based social pressures in hopes of garnering acceptance and securing positive social standings during the establishment of new peer groups (e.g., Smith-Jackson, Reel, & Thackeray, 2011). Thirdly, data collected from relatively racially-homogenous participant samples suggests that White college women more generally (Bailey, Lamarche, & Gammage, 2014; Lamarche, Kerr, Faulkner, Gammage, & Klentrou, 2012) and first-year females in particular (Smith-Jackson et al., 2011) are susceptible to engaging in experientially-avoidant coping responses while confronting body image threats (Cash et al., 2005) as a means of averting shame and other forms of negative social evaluation (Bailey et al., 2014). Alternatively, a concerning minority of young women reported turning to positive rational acceptance (Cash et al., 2005) to combat everyday body image challenges while acclimating to the college environment (Smith-Jackson et al., 2011). Lastly, it was deemed beneficial to focus this first-stage investigation on young women representing this particular socio-demographic group in light of evidence indicating that among predominantly White college participants, females relative to their male counterparts tend to endorse lower levels of body image flexibility (e.g., Sandoz et al., 2013) and body appreciation (e.g., Tylka, 2013) in conjunction with more frequently utilizing avoidant coping strategies in handling body image threats and challenges (Cash et al., 2005).

A secondary aim of the present investigation was to advance the existing literature by operationalizing body dissatisfaction utilizing a broader range of externally valid body size comparison referents. Myriad scholarship conventionally limits defining body dissatisfaction to the subjective discrepancy endorsed between an individual's current body size and her ideal body size using visual figure rating scales (e.g., see Roberts et al. (2006) for a meta-analytic review). However, some experts now contend that a singular emphasis on anchoring body dissatisfaction in reference to an internalized personal standard fails to adequately account for body image distress stemming from comparison to external cultural group ideals (e.g., those promulgated in the media) nor to typical female peers encountered during the course of participating in everyday interactions (e.g., Forbes, Adams-Curtis, Rade, & Jaberg, 2001; Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2011; Gordon, Castro, Sitnikov, & Holm-Denoma, 2010; Krones, Stice, Batres, & Orjada, 2005; Ridolfi, Myers, Crowther, & Ciesla, 2011; Strahan, Wilson, Cressman, & Buote, 2006). Indeed, in today's technology-driven culture, adolescent young women preparing to transition to college life arguably face a perpetual onslaught of exposure to both of these body-size comparison referent sources as a consequence of the ubiquity of modern social media (e.g., Chrisler, Fung, Lopez, & Gorman, 2013; Perloff, 2014).

In sum, young White women on the cusp of entering college may be at elevated risk for coping with body image threats in experientially-avoidant ways. The present study sought to further unpack the linkages among three types of body size discrepancies (i.e., current minus personal ideal, current minus cultural group ideal, and current minus typical female ethnic peer) and two forms of contemporary positive body image. Based on an expansion of the affect regulation model of positive body image (Webb et al., 2014), it was predicted that controlling for body mass index (BMI), body image flexibility would at least partially mediate the relationships between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation in all three models tested in an initial-stage sample of White collegebound females.

The research described here is drawn from a larger data set sponsored by an NIH grant designed to better understand the biopsychosocial determinants of weight gain among first-year college women. After receiving the appropriate ethical approvals, our pre-college sample was recruited via letters sent through the mail as well as electronically to all young women who racially identified as White or Caucasian from a list of all admitted females received from the Office of Admissions of our large state-funded southeastern U.S. university. Prospective participants were urged to obtain a parent or other primary adult caregiver's consent before completing the online survey administered through Survey-Share. As an incentive, participants' names were entered into a drawing for one of 3 iPad 2s. The questionnaires were presented in a fixed order format in the sequence they are described in further detail below. Only the measures relevant to addressing this study's primary aims are presented. Participants completed a series of additional measures not directly pertinent to the current analysis' key objectives, the results of which are described elsewhere (Webb, Butler-Ajibade, Robinson, & Lee, 2013). Participants' survey responses were de-identified though not completely anonymous as their study identification numbers were linked to their names and contact information in a master tracking file given that this phase of the study was intended to be the first data collection time point as part of a longitudinal investigation.

Ninety-four White older adolescent females aged 17–19 admitted to the university completed the brief online survey during the summer before they started college. This number reflects a relatively modest response rate of 8% based on the initial number of approximately 1200 recruitment invitations sent out to prospective students. However, data from 10 participants were excluded due to missing data (please see the results section below for additional details) resulting in a final sample size of 84 participants (mean age=17.9 years, SD=.37) with complete data on which the primary analyses were performed. On average, respondents reported a BMI of 22.7 (SD=3.9) falling within the normal range. Based on CDC (n.d.) guidelines, the BMI distribution of the sample was as follows: 6.2% underweight, 70.4% normal weight, 19.8% overweight, and 3.6% obese.

The demographic component of the web survey requested participants' age along with height (in feet and inches) and weight (in lbs.) which were used to calculate BMI according to the following standard algorithm: weight (lb.)/[height (in.)]^2 \times 703.

Participants completed the 12-item Body Image-Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (BI-AAQ; Sandoz et al., 2013) as a measure of body image flexibility. Respondents use a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (never true) to 7 (always true) to rate the degree to which they willingly and non-judgmentally make contact with negative thoughts and emotions related to the body and/or weight as opposed to trying to eliminate or control these internal experiences in the service of pursuing valued living. All items are negatively-keyed (e.g., "Before I can make any serious plans, I have to feel better about my body.") and therefore are reverse-scored resulting in higher scores reflecting higher levels of body image flexibility (or lower levels of body image experiential avoidance; see Webb et al. (2015) for a discussion and critique). Scale developers reported excellent internal consistency reliability (\alpha=.93) in

their initial validation work with undergraduate students (Sandoz et al., 2013). In the present sample, an alpha of .92 was achieved. Mean scores of 66.6 (SD=15.1) and 67.4 (SD=12.0) were reported in non-clinical samples of U.S. college students (Sandoz et al., 2013) and Portuguese adults (Ferreira et al., 2011) respectively. Ferreira et al. (2011) additionally observed an average BI-AAQ score of 31.4 (SD=1.8) in a small sample of eating disorder patients.

Participants completed the 13-item first-generation Body Appreciation Scale (BAS: Avalos et al., 2005) as a measure of valuesconsistent action in the context of positive body image. Participants utilize a 5-point scale with anchors ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always) to rate the extent to which they accept, respect, protect, and take care of their bodies. Higher scores represent greater levels of body appreciation (e.g., "Despite its flaws, I accept my body for what it is."). Avalos et al. (2005) reported superior levels of internal consistency (\alpha = .94) in their original undergraduate female validation sample. Among current participants, internal consistency exceeded acceptable limits (\alpha=.93). Researchers noted an average BAS score of 3.48 (SD=.79) in a non-clinical sample of U.S. female college students. While Bush, Rossy, Mintz, and Schopp (2014) observed a mean baseline BAS score of 2.82 (SD=.67) among U.S. adult women preparing to participate in a mindfulness and intuitive eating based intervention for individuals with problematic eating behavior though means by clinical cut-offs on a diagnostic measure of disordered eating were not published (Bush et al., 2014).

Pulvers and colleagues' figure rating scale was used to obtain participants' body size ratings for their current body size, their personal ideal body size, their cultural group ideal body size, and for the body size of a typical female peer from their cultural group (Pulvers et al., 2004). This measure presents respondents with nine female images increasing in body size depicted with ethnically-neutral hair and facial features. Three body size discrepancy body dissatisfaction scores were computed: current minus personal ideal, current minus cultural ideal and current minus typical female ethnic peer. No specific guidance was given to participants for determining who to use in estimating body size perceptions for their cultural group ideal or a typical female peer from their racial/ ethnic group. Thus, participants were free to use their subjective interpretations of these items accordingly. The strong psychometric properties inclusive of criterion, concurrent, and convergent validity in conjunction with inter-rater reliability of this measure are detailed in the original validation paper (Pulvers et al., 2004). Webb et al. (2014) observed the following means for each body size discrepancy in a sample of Black older adolescent females: current minus personal ideal: .52 (SD=1.2), current minus cultural ideal: .22 (SD=1.6), and current minus typical female ethnic peer: -.54 (SD=1.7). To this author's knowledge this particular figure rating scale remains to be evaluated in clinical samples or those who are at-risk for a clinical disorder.

Data were screened for amount of missingness and to ensure that the distributional characteristics of the variables met normative assumptions prior to executing formal statistical analytic procedures. The amount of missing data at the variable level ranged from 0% to 9%. In order to provide the most conservative test of our hypotheses, complete case analyses were conducted, although the limitations of this approach to handling missing data

Skewness ( < 3.0) and kurtosis ( < 10.0) values fell within the acceptable ranges as recommended by Kline (2010) and therefore no data transformations were performed. Nonetheless, as will be described below, the use of non-parametric bootstrapping approaches are more robust to departures of normality, and such procedures generate reliable parameter estimates with smaller sample sizes (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). Indeed, according to Fritz and MacKinnon's (2007) guidelines, a sample size of 84 well exceeds the recommended threshold of 53 required to detect the combination of a medium (i.e., the alpha path coefficient is .39) by large (i.e., the beta path coefficient is .59) size mediational effect at 80% power using bias-corrected bootstrap resampling estimating procedures.

Table 1 presents the means, standard deviations and the correlational matrix for the primary study variables. Both measures of positive body image were highly positively correlated. All three forms of body dissatisfaction discrepancy scores were strongly inversely related to both body appreciation and body image flexibility scores. The BMI of participants was positively associated with all three metrics of body dissatisfaction. Finally, possessing a higher BMI on the cusp of entering college corresponded with lower body image flexibility affect regulation skills and less frequent engagement in body appreciation valued actions. All correlations were in the expected directions.

To evaluate the hypotheses that body image flexibility at least partially mediated the relationships between the three forms of body dissatisfaction and body appreciation, non-parametric bootstrap resampling procedures were computed utilizing the SPSS INDIRECT custom dialog (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). All variables were standardized using z-scores prior to being entered into each model. Total, direct and indirect effect estimates were produced. Ten thousand bootstrap resamples were performed for each of the three models. Additionally, the significance at the p < .05 level of the bias-corrected 95% CI for each indirect effect was determined in the case where zero was not included. Initially, models were computed unadjusted for BMI and then subsequently analyzed while including BMI as a covariate. This was done in order to determine whether BMI impacted the strength of original indirect effects. Fig. 1 Panels A, B, and C provide graphical representations of these results for the unadjusted models.

Additionally, these indirect effects were robust to inclusion of BMI regardless of the particular body size discrepancy predictor. Specifically, the indirect effect of the current-personal ideal body size discrepancy on body appreciation scores via body image flexibility was highly significant and was observed as \beta = -.34 (95% CI = -.50 to -.22). The total effect of body dissatisfaction in this model was estimated as \beta = -.59, t(83) = -6.76, p < .001. This association remained intact when adjusted for BMI: indirect effect \beta = -.33 (95% CI = -.55 to -.17). Similarly, with respect to the current-cultural ideal body dissatisfaction model, the indirect

effect was estimated to be β¼ .33 (95% CI¼ .51 to .20). The total effect of body dissatisfaction in this second model was observed as β¼ .50, t(83)¼ 4.95, po.001. As seen in the previous model, the significance of the indirect effect was retained when controlling for BMI, β¼ .26 (95% CI¼ .48 to .08). Finally, body image flexibility partially mediated the relationship between current-typical female ethnic peer body dissatisfaction scores and body appreciation: β¼ .28 (95% CI¼ .43 to .15). The total effect of this type of body size discrepancy score on body appreciation was shown to be β¼ .44, t(83)¼ 4.45, po.001. Consistent with the previously reported results, this indirect effect was preserved when BMI was included as a covariate in the model, β¼ .18 (95% CI¼ .38 to .01).

Guided from an emergent affect regulation model of positive body image (Webb et al., 2014) as applied to the context of coping with body image threats (e.g., Cash, 2002; Cash et al., 2005), the present study evaluated whether body image flexibility mediated the associations between three types of body size discrepancies and body appreciation in a pre-college sample of White older adolescent females. In support of this objective, across all models tested, results confirmed that compassionately and mindfully confronting aversive thoughts and emotions related to the body served to partially explain the inverse relationships between body dissatisfaction and engaging in body appreciation conceptualized here as valued action (Webb et al., 2014). Notably, findings were retained when controlling for BMI.

These preliminary findings help expand current theoretical (e.g., Cash, 2002; Webb et al., 2014) and empirical (e.g., Atkinson & Wade, 2012; Cash et al., 2005; Dijkstra & Barelds, 2011; Swami, Salem, Furnham, & Tovee, 2008; Svaldi et al., 2013) understandings of the relationships between negative and positive body image as they unfold within individuals. Grounded within a broader psychological flexibility theoretical framework (Hayes et al., 1999), results additionally offer unique insights into how two components of positive body image may possibly function in relation to one another in the process of managing body dissatisfaction arising from appearance-related social comparisons and self-discrepancies in order to promote values-congruent action in this context. Though a more comprehensive evaluation of these proposed causal relationships warrants further investigation using experimental research methodology.

The observed effects also extend previous cross-sectional (e.g., Ferreira et al., 2011; Ferreira et al., 2015; Sandoz et al., 2013; Timko et al., 2014; Wendell et al., 2012) research citing body image flexibility as a useful process in possibly mitigating risk of disordered eating in the presence of body dissatisfaction. In line with this emerging evidence in the domain of eating behavior, body image flexibility may also be instrumental in promoting body appreciation when confronting challenges to body image. Later experimental and/or longitudinal research will be useful in confirming whether the combination of body image flexibility and body appreciation helps improve the reduction of risk for eating disturbances that would be predicted by body dissatisfaction in vulnerable populations such as college women. Conversely, perhaps subsequent evidence may emerge suggesting that it may be the synergistic (rather than independent) effect of these two contemporary forms of positive body image that best contribute to more frequently engaging in adaptive eating processes in circumstances involving the heightened experiential activation of body image-related stress.
Nonetheless, while much research has tended to emphasize the critical importance of negative body image as a risk factor for

disordered eating (e.g., Stice et al., 1998), this study contributes to the growing scientific base suggesting the value of focusing on positive body image characteristics as worthy outcomes to strive towards in and of themselves in promoting health and well-being in addition to their potential links to preventing serious psychological disorders (e.g., Bush et al., 2014; Cotter, Kelly, Mitchell, & Mazzeo, 2015; Homan & Cavanaugh, 2013; Homan & Tylka, 2014; Homan & Tylka, 2015; Tiggemann, Coutts, & Clark, 2014; Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014; Wasylkiw, MacKinnon, & MacLellan, 2012; Webb et al., 2014). Indeed, research has supported body appreciation as a predictor and/or intermediary process in the prediction of a range of health-related criterion variables (e.g., Andrew et al., 2014; Avalos & Tylka, 2006; Augustus-Horvath & Tylka, 2011; Gillen, 2015; see Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a for an overview). Yet, the stage is set to continue to uncover what factors contribute to the development, strength and durability of this dimension of positive body image with body image flexibility now considered as a potential candidate alongside self-compassion (Homan & Tylka, 2015; Wasylkiw et al., 2012). Incorporating the fusion of psychological flexibility (Hayes et al., 1999) and coping with body image threats (Cash et al., 2005) theoretical frameworks may serve as a useful template for translating these concepts into the promotion of positive body image in a diverse range of applied contexts (Callaghan et al., 2015).

For example, these initial-stage findings may have implications for supporting college health promotion efforts for incoming young women that prioritize a focus on bolstering positive body image self-regulatory skills as a means to adaptively respond to everyday instances of body image threats as they acclimate to early college life. Results tentatively suggest that emphasis on cultivating body image flexibility could serve as a beneficial alternative to the default experiential avoidant approach to coping with body image stressors frequently reported among young women during this particular developmental transition (e.g., Bailey et al., 2014; Cash et al., 2005; Lamarche et al., 2012; Smith-Jackson et al., 2011). Doing so may raise the potential to choose to engage in values-congruent action in the moment in the form of body appreciation (e.g., eating intuitively versus binge eating; Schoenefeld & Webb, 2013). These speculations though promising would clearly need to be further substantiated in subsequent intervention research with this target population.

Another suggested future research direction involves giving a fuller consideration of the potential role of positive rational acceptance coping (Callaghan et al., 2015; Cash et al., 2005) in this context. Indeed, this highly relevant line of inquiry would seem a fruitful avenue to pursue given the contribution of Cash et al.'s (2005) framework to the current analysis' theoretical underpinnings in conjunction with its recent application in attempting to better clarify how college women in particular cope with body image distress (e.g., Bailey et al., 2014; Lamarche et al., 2012; Smith-Jackson et al., 2011). Additionally, it is apparent that body image flexibility and positive rational acceptance coping demonstrate convergence in both theoretical foundations and in the overlapping item content of their instrumentation. Thus, in line with recent recommendations (Webb et al., 2015) and scholarship (Callaghan et al., 2015), it would appear advantageous for subsequent efforts to further examine the ways in which both of these positive body image attributes relate to one another and to evaluate the extent to which positive rational acceptance comparably serves to assist in explaining the links between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation among older adolescent females preparing for college matriculation.

Limitations of the present study include the relatively small, racially-homogenous, non-random sample and the cross-sectional study design which precludes making causal inferences. Thus, later-stage investigations utilizing prospective and/or experimental

methodology are recommended towards further confirming the validity of the models tested here. Moreover, the body size (e.g., thin, average, overweight) of the typical female ethnic peer referent was not specified (Lin & Kulik, 2002) which could possibly affect the directionality of the body size comparisons made (e.g., upward versus downward) by young women of varying weight statuses. The rather low response rate to the survey (likely in part a result of the incentive structure) also limits the generalizability of findings. Future research would benefit from evaluating this affect regulation process model within larger, more ethnically-, gender-, regionally-, and economically-diverse older adolescent samples to assess whether the observed effects are robust to these aspects of cultural variation. The reliance on the use of self-report measures is an additional shortcoming to acknowledge as more generally responses may reflect inattentiveness and inaccurate perceptions and in the specific case of BMI may have contributed to over- or under-reporting. Moreover, the possibility of order effects in contributing to the current findings cannot be fully discounted due to the lack of administering the surveys in a random or counterbalanced sequence. The lack of participant anonymity may have additionally impacted the accuracy of reporting. Lastly, while discrepancy-based figure rating scale scores are frequently used to measure body dissatisfaction (e.g., Roberts et al., 2006), other scholars debate whether this is a valid representation of the construct (e.g., Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2011). Therefore subsequent investigations are encouraged to incorporate body dissatisfaction instruments within the models tested here that also more explicitly tap into the importance and affective components of body dissatisfaction as has been featured in previous research (e.g., Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2011; Gordon et al., 2010). Nevertheless, despite these caveats, this study's preliminary results may have the potential to enhance affect regulation-based theoretical models linking body dissatisfaction to positive body image that in turn could be translated into promoting body image resilience (Snapp, Hensley-Choate, & Ryu, 2012) and other constructive approaches to handling everyday challenges to body image at this unique developmental juncture.
